label: Packaged app (local install from a public GitHub release)
summary: An application people install on their own machine from a signed package published as a GitHub release. Not cloud deployed. Examples: the Mac and Raspberry Pi control dashboards.
planner_text: Saved scope, exclusions, explicit story-model preference and selected delivery take precedence over template examples. Never introduce an unrequested form/backend/tracking feature. First check coordinator readiness; correct plan prerequisites using save/replan and linked approved host controls. This is a packaged app delivered as a signed package from a public GitHub release and installed locally; it is not cloud deployed. Plan the work as small stories with tests. The release flow is fixed and belongs to the operator's approval: changelog and version bump, a pull request with green CI, merge, tag, a package built and signed by the release workflow, verification of the checksum, signature and manifest, and publishing the verified draft. Agents prepare the code, tests, docs and changelog; they do not publish a release, hold a signing key or install onto the operator's machine. Plan a verification story that checks the built package, a human story to test an install and an update on the target hardware, and a human story that approves publishing. The update path, migrations and anything that touches the installer are high risk. No personal information, keys, hostnames or paths from the operator's machine may be in the packaged files. If the app has screens, add a file-level verification story and an automated preview-verification checkpoint (set host_action to "preview-verify"; the separate human review story uses host_action "preview-review") before a human sign-off; the verifier captures URLs and screenshots where available, checks the health endpoint and each page, records the commit and results, then shuts down its own preview. Never ask an agent story to render pages, check a browser console or take screenshots: agent sandboxes have no browser, so keep agent verification static and leave rendering to the human preview. The project ends in the remote repository, not in a scratch folder: when the brief names a repository, the working folder must be a clone of it, and the plan needs a delivery story that pushes the project branch and opens a pull request, then a story that reads the pipeline result so the image or app build and the tests have actually run there. Nothing goes to the main branch from an agent. The project is not done until the branch is pushed, the pull request is open and the pipeline result is known. The repository is public: this app is delivered as an MIT-licensed package that other people install from a GitHub release, so its code, tests and pipeline are public too. Say the licence in the plan. Plan the documentation as part of the project: a README story (an agent writes it) and the how-tos, with a Mermaid architecture diagram and a data-flow diagram whenever the project is more than a local install, and a screenshot of every application area plus how-tos for what a person does beyond installing and signing in. Screenshots are made with Playwright from a script kept in the repository, run by a person or a CI job against seeded test data, because agent sandboxes have no browser; the agent writes the script and the README, a human story or the pipeline runs it and commits the images.
failure_points: The release is the operator's approval: an agent must not publish, sign or install; plan those as human stories.
Code that must run on older target Python versions needs a compile check for that version before it is pushed, or CI fails.
Personal information, keys, hostnames and local paths must never ship in a package; scan before release.
The update path is high risk; it needs a human install and update test on the target hardware.
Actions minutes cost money: batch non-blocking fixes and release only for a verified blocker.
A restart or upgrade of a running install must wait until nothing is running.

A story that asks an agent to render pages, read a browser console or take screenshots cannot be done in an agent sandbox (no browser, no loopback server); it reports itself unfinished and blocks everything behind it. Agent verification is static (files, references, syntax, tests); rendering is checked by a person in the preview.

A project run in a scratch folder with no git remote finishes with nothing pushed: no pull request and no pipeline run, so the image or app build and tests never ran where they are meant to. When the brief names a repository, the working folder must be a clone of it, and delivery (push the project branch, open the pull request, read the pipeline result) must be stories in the plan.

A README with only install commands tells a new person nothing about the application. Add a Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagram when it is more than a local install, a screenshot and a short how-to for each application area beyond installation and sign-in, and make the screenshots with a Playwright script that a person or the pipeline runs (an agent cannot run a browser).
visual_checks: Screens get a file-level verification story, then an automated preview-verification checkpoint that captures screenshots or a local URL and shuts down cleanly, then a human sign-off.
human_signoffs: Install and update test on the target hardware
Anything touching the update path or installer
How a screen looks (after a preview)

checks.message: Publishing, signing and installing belong to the operator. Make this a human story.
No human install or update test on the target hardware.
No human story approves publishing the release.
Publishing comes before any package verification story.

A story asks an agent to render pages or check a browser console, which no agent sandbox can do. It will report itself unfinished. Keep agent verification to static checks and move rendering to the human preview.

No delivery story. A project should end in the remote repository: add a story that pushes the project branch and opens a pull request, and one that reads the pipeline result (the build and tests running there), or say plainly that this project has no repository.
No README or documentation story. Add one that writes the README with a Mermaid architecture and data-flow diagram (when it is more than a local install) and a how-to for each application area.

No story that makes the application screenshots. Agents cannot run a browser: add a human story (or a pipeline job) that runs the Playwright screenshot script against seeded test data and commits the images the README uses.
